text.text: Background: Advanced epithelial ovarian cancer disproportionately affects older women.
While primary debulking surgery (PDS) is the traditional gold standard, it carries substantial morbidity and mortality risks in frail, older patients.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery (NACT-IDS) can downstage disease and mitigate these surgical risks, but high-level evidence syntheses specific to geriatric populations remain limited.
Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261461644).

Five electronic databases and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for comparative studies evaluating NACT-IDS versus PDS in women aged 70 years (or 65 years in defined geriatric cohorts) with FIGO Stage IIIC/IV epithelial ovarian cancer.
Outcomes were synthesized using random-effects models.
Methodological quality was assessed via the ROBINS-I tool, cumulative evidence reliability via Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA), and overall evidence certainty via the GRADE framework.
Results: Eleven retrospective cohort studies encompassing over 16,500 older patients met the inclusion criteria.
NACT-IDS yielded an 80% reduction in unadjusted 30-day perioperative mortality compared to PDS (RR = 0.20, 95% CI [0.05, 0.89], p = 0.034).

Furthermore, NACT-IDS significantly decreased hospital length of stay (MD = -3.12 days, p = 0.0044) and increased the likelihood of complete macroscopic resection (R0 = 0 cm) by 74% (RR = 1.74, 95% CI [1.01, 3.02], p = 0.047).
Severe complications (Clavien-Dindo 3) trended lower with NACT-IDS (RR = 0.38, 95% CI [0.13, 1.08]).

Unadjusted overall survival models demonstrated a 13% increased hazard of death for NACT-IDS (HR = 1.13, 95% CI [1.04, 1.23]); however, this primarily reflects profound selection bias (confounding by indication) where the frailest patients were systematically triaged to the NACT-IDS pathway.
The overall certainty of evidence was appraised as Very Low.

Conclusion: For older women with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, NACT-IDS significantly improves perioperative safety, accelerates hospital recovery, and maximizes complete resection rates compared to upfront PDS.

While retrospective survival data are heavily skewed by channeling bias, NACT-IDS effectively protects physiological reserve and should be strongly considered as the standard initial management strategy for this vulnerable demographic.

text.text: Aging drives a progressive loss of stress tolerance, rooted in the depletion of functional organ reserve and the erosion of personal and social resources (2).
The cardiovascular, renal, pulmonary, central nervous, and skeletomuscular systems lose capacity over time, fundamentally altering physiological responses to stress (6).
Renal function can decline by 40% by age 70.
This drop in glomerular filtration rate directly amplifies the toxicity of renally excreted agents like cisplatin (3).
Altered geriatric physiology shifts the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of all systemic medications, particularly anesthetics (6).

While these age-related physiological changes may remain clinically silent under homeostatic conditions, acute surgical or cytotoxic stress rapidly exposes the underlying lack of functional reserve (9).

text.text: Frailty operates as a complex biological syndrome defined by exhausted physiological reserve and an inability to withstand stressors, leaving the patient highly vulnerable to adverse outcomes (4).

text.text: The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to definitively evaluate the perioperative safety, surgical morbidity, and oncological outcomes of NACT-IDS compared to PDS, specifically in older women (age ≥70 years) with advanced (FIGO Stage IIIC-IV) epithelial ovarian cancer.
We hypothesize that NACT-IDS mitigates the physiological insult of radical cytoreduction, thereby reducing severe postoperative complications and short-term mortality in this vulnerable demographic.
This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in rigorous adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines.
The predefined methodology was prospectively registered in the PROSPERO International Register of Systematic Reviews (Registration No.
The Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes (PICO) framework was utilized to define inclusion criteria.

Studies were eligible if they included: (P) female patients designated as elderly (defined as chronological age 70 years, or 65 years if explicitly analyzed as a distinct geriatric cohort) with advanced-stage (FIGO IIIC/IV) epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal carcinoma; (I) treatment with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery (NACT-IDS); (C) comparison to primary debulking surgery (PDS); and (O) reported on at least one primary safety outcome (perioperative mortality, severe Clavien-Dindo 3 complications), surgical efficacy outcome (complete macroscopic resection, R0 = 0 cm), or survival metric (Overall Survival [OS]).
Exclusion criteria encompassed noncomparative single-arm studies, case reports, cohorts lacking isolated geriatric data, and studies analyzing non-epithelial histologies.

A comprehensive, systematic literature search was executed without language restrictions across five electronic databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Google Scholar.
To identify unpublished or ongoing trials, ClinicalTrials.gov was also queried.

The search strategy utilized a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text keywords encompassing the population ("Elderly", "Geriatric", "Aged"), intervention ("Neoadjuvant Therapy", "NACT", "Interval Debulking"), comparator ("Primary Debulking", "PDS", "Cytoreductive Surgery"), and disease state ("Ovarian Neoplasms", "Epithelial Ovarian Cancer").
Retrieved citations were imported into EndNote for deduplication and subsequently transferred to the Rayyan web application for screening.
Two investigators independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text evaluation of potentially eligible records.
Discrepancies were resolved via consensus or consultation with a third senior investigator.
Data extraction was performed independently using standardized collection forms, capturing study parameters, patient demographics, surgical variables, and clinical outcomes.

Because the final included literature consisted entirely of non-randomized comparative cohort studies, methodological quality was assessed using the Risk Of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies -of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool.

Studies were evaluated across seven domains: confounding, selection of participants, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, measurement of outcomes, and selection of the reported result.
Visual summaries of bias risk were generated.
Meta-analytic synthesis was performed using the meta package in R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing).
Given the anticipated clinical heterogeneity inherent in global surgical practices and geriatric definitions, random-effects models were utilized universally.
Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the statistic and Cochrane's Q test, with values 75% considered high heterogeneity.
• Binary Outcomes: Pooled as Relative Risks (RR) with 95% Confidence Intervals (CI) utilizing the Mantel-Haenszel method.

For rare safety endpoints (e.g., perioperative mortality), in accordance with Cochrane methodological guidelines, the routine 0.5 continuity correction was omitted for "double-zero" studies in the primary analysis to prevent the artificial dilution of the effect size toward the null.
Penalized models incorporating the continuity correction were executed as sensitivity analyses.

• Continuous Outcomes: Variables such as hospital length of stay (days) were synthesized as Mean Differences (MD) using the generic inverse-variance method and the Restricted Maximum-Likelihood (REML) estimator for betweenstudy variance ( ).
Imputation of standard deviations from medians and ranges was performed when necessary for sensitivity testing.
• Survival Outcomes: Time-to-event data (OS) were pooled as Hazard Ratios (HR) using the generic inverse-variance method.

To control for the risks of Type I (false positive) and Type II (false negative) errors inherent in cumulative meta-analyses, and to assess whether the accrued geriatric sample size was sufficient, Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) was performed.
The Diversity-Adjusted Required Information Size (DARIS) was calculated using an alpha of 5% and a beta of 20% (80% power).

O'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending monitoring boundaries were constructed to determine if the cumulative Z-curve crossed into areas of definitive clinical benefit or harm prior to reaching the required information size.
The overall certainty of the body of evidence was appraised using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.

Outcomes were graded as High, Moderate, Low, or Very Low certainty based on the observational nature of the starting evidence, combined with downgrades for serious risk of bias (confounding), inconsistency (heterogeneity), indirectness, and imprecision (evaluated via TSA thresholds).
The initial literature search yielded 4,691 records.
We removed 1,731 duplicates and screened the remaining 2,960 records by abstract.
Investigators sought 173 full-text articles for retrieval and fully assessed 161 for eligibility.
We excluded 150 articles, primarily due to a lack of separate elderly data (n = 123) or the absence of a direct comparison (n = 20).
The final quantitative synthesis included 11 retrospective cohort studies comprising over 16,500 elderly patients (Figure 1).

text.text: This meta-analysis demonstrates that in older women with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, NACT-IDS profoundly alters the perioperative safety profile compared to upfront PDS.

The utilization of neoadjuvant chemotherapy yielded an 80% unadjusted reduction in 30-day perioperative mortality, significantly decreased hospital length of stay, and drove a 74% increase in the likelihood of achieving complete macroscopic (R0) cytoreduction.

Despite these overwhelming perioperative advantages, unadjusted survival models demonstrated a superficial hazard favoring PDS, an observation that directly reflects severe confounding by indication rather than true oncological inferiority.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) actively reduces tumor burden, resolves tissue reactive edema, and disrupts dense adhesions between malignant deposits and adjacent viscera.
This pharmacological downstaging establishes a highly favorable environment for effective cytoreduction (32).
text.formatted: This pharmacological downstaging establishes a highly favorable environment for effective cytoreduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(32)</ref>.

text.text: By contracting the physical extent of the disease, NACT increases the technical feasibility of complete macroscopic resection.
Intraoperative data confirm this effect.
The incidence of metastatic deposits exceeding 5 cm at the time of surgery drops by half in NACT cohorts compared to primary debulking surgery (PDS) cohorts (37.2% versus 74.5%) (33).
text.formatted: The incidence of metastatic deposits exceeding 5 cm at the time of surgery drops by half in NACT cohorts compared to primary debulking surgery (PDS) cohorts (37.2% versus 74.5%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(33)</ref>.

This strategy inherently limits surgical morbidity (37).

text.text: The NACT-IDS paradigm yields fewer surgical complications, reduced operative mortality, lower estimated blood loss, decreased ascites volume, shorter operative times, accelerated hospital discharge, and superior postoperative quality of life.
Conversely, PDS demands higher surgical complexity.

This aggressive upfront approach drives elevated rates of grade 3 or 4 surgical complications, postoperative infections, wound dehiscence, vascular events, intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, reoperations, and readmissions (16).

text.text: Quantitative metrics strongly favor the delayed surgical approach.

Compared to primary cytoreduction, interval procedures require significantly less operative time (median reduction of 35 min; p = 0.01), generate less intraoperative hemorrhage (median reduction of 382 mL; p < 0.001), and require shorter inpatient admissions (median reduction of 5 days; p = 0.002) (38).

text.text: Following two to three cycles of neoadjuvant treatment, patients typically reverse cachexia, demonstrating weight gain, improved functional status, and rising serum albumin levels.
NACT effectively clears pleural effusions and massive ascites.
This physiological optimization permits the surgeon to execute maximal cytoreductive efforts with acceptable morbidity profiles (6).

text.text: Clinical data confirm this restorative effect.
Women receiving 3-4 cycles of NACT exhibit a dramatic increase in ECOG 0 performance status (53.3% vs 81.8%; p < 0.001) and median serum albumin levels (3.0 g/dl vs 4.0 g/dl; p < 0.001).

text.text: This prehabilitation translates directly to the operating room.

Severe postoperative complications occur significantly less frequently in patients treated with 3-4 NACT cycles (5.4% vs 18.6%; p = 0.0003) or 6 NACT cycles (7.8% vs 18.6%; p = 0.053) compared to upfront surgery cohorts.
NACT actively modifies baseline risk factors, converting initially inoperable, high-risk patients into viable surgical candidates (40).

text.text: By simultaneously eradicating ascites to improve surgical tolerance and shrinking solid tumors to facilitate optimal debulking, NACT systematically improves the patient's physiological readiness for major abdominal surgery (17, 40).

text.text: Observational cohort studies suffer from profound selection bias.
Retrospective analyses consistently demonstrate that NACT cohorts are significantly older and present less frequently with stage III disease compared to PDS cohorts.
While propensity score matching attempts to control for this bias, unmeasured confounding variables heavily concentrate in the NACT population, artificially depressing their survival figures (33).
text.formatted: While propensity score matching attempts to control for this bias, unmeasured confounding variables heavily concentrate in the NACT population, artificially depressing their survival figures <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(33)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians triage patients to primary surgery or NACT based on initial clinical and radiological severity.
Consequently, NACT cohorts inherently possess massive tumor burdens, advanced age, extreme baseline CA-125 elevations, and a disproportionate volume of stage IV disease.
These patients frequently present with ECOG performance scores of 3-4 and severe medical comorbidities.
This nonhomogeneous distribution of baseline characteristics guarantees a biased comparison (41).
text.formatted: This nonhomogeneous distribution of baseline characteristics guarantees a biased comparison <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(41)</ref>.

text.text: Surgeons systematically channel elderly patients and those with heavy comorbidity burdens toward NACT.

Institutional and patient-level factors driving NACT utilization include advanced age, frailty, serous or unclassified histology, stage IV presentation, massive disease dissemination, insurance status, geographical distance from the treatment center, institutional adoption of NACT protocols, and adherence to NCCN guidelines (16).

text.text: Real-world clinical practice naturally segregates patients.
Individuals receiving NACT are fundamentally older, frailer, and burdened with more extensive disease than those undergoing primary cytoreduction (42).
text.formatted: Individuals receiving NACT are fundamentally older, frailer, and burdened with more extensive disease than those undergoing primary cytoreduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(42)</ref>.

text.text: Severe comorbidities and poor functional status independently dictate a dismal prognosis regardless of the chosen therapeutic modality, and these exact factors trigger the clinical decision to initiate NACT.
The survival advantage frequently attributed to primary surgery in observational literature stems directly from inadequate statistical adjustment for baseline physiological health.
When outcome models properly adjust for specific cognitive and frailty indices, the spurious association between NACT and increased all-cause mortality disappears (43).
text.formatted: When outcome models properly adjust for specific cognitive and frailty indices, the spurious association between NACT and increased all-cause mortality disappears <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(43)</ref>.

text.text: Surgeons preferentially select NACT for patients exhibiting frailty, severe medical conditions, poor performance status, and FIGO stage IV disease.
These exact clinicopathological variables independently drive poor survival.
Failing to account for this baseline disparity severely underestimates the true survival outcomes of the interval cytoreductive approach (38).

Mortality scales aggressively with advancing age.

Postoperative fatal complications occur in 9% of octogenarians, compared to just 1% of patients under 60.
Relative to patients younger than 60, the odds ratio for 30-day postoperative mortality rises to 3.7 for ages 60-69, 3.1 for ages 70-79, and peaks at 9.3 for patients aged 80 and older.
Octogenarians presenting with extensive disease requiring four-quadrant peritoneal resection require alternative strategies, specifically neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by delayed debulking.
For profoundly frail patients burdened with multiple comorbidities, primary chemotherapy without surgical intervention represents the most appropriate pathway (6).
text.formatted: For profoundly frail patients burdened with multiple comorbidities, primary chemotherapy without surgical intervention represents the most appropriate pathway <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: Surgical intervention in extreme age groups yields grim statistics.
A retrospective analysis of 85 patients over 80 undergoing cytoreductive surgery revealed a 13% inhospital mortality rate, with 20% of the cohort dying within 60 days of the operation (47).
text.formatted: A retrospective analysis of 85 patients over 80 undergoing cytoreductive surgery revealed a 13% inhospital mortality rate, with 20% of the cohort dying within 60 days of the operation <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(47)</ref>.

text.text: Overall surgical complication rates climb linearly with age, rising from 17.1% in patients under 50 to 31.5% in those 80 and older (48).
text.formatted: Overall surgical complication rates climb linearly with age, rising from 17.1% in patients under 50 to 31.5% in those 80 and older <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(48)</ref>.

text.text: Loss of independence follows a similar trajectory.
Discharge to a skilled nursing facility occurs in only 1.0% of patients under 50, but jumps to 14.0% for patients aged 70 to 79, and reaches 33.3% for patients older than 80 (3).
This study represents the most comprehensive quantitative synthesis of geriatric ovarian cancer surgery to date.
The methodology departs from traditional metaanalyses by integrating advanced error-control frameworks.

The application of Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) objectively maps the boundaries of required information size, preventing premature declarations of superiority based on underpowered observational cohorts.

Furthermore, the rigorous application of the ROBINS-I tool and the GRADE framework provides absolute transparency regarding the certainty of the current evidence base, specifically highlighting the pervasive issue of selection bias in retrospective gynecologic oncology literature.
The primary limitation of this meta-analysis is the inherent reliance on observational, retrospective cohort studies.

This introduces profound channeling bias, as surgeons naturally triage the oldest, frailest, and highest-tumor-burden patients to NACT, while reserving PDS for robust, physiologically younger seniors.
Because the baseline denominators are fundamentally unequal, direct survival comparisons are inherently flawed without universal propensity-score matching.
Additionally, the included literature relies entirely on chronological age cutoffs (e.g., ≥70 years).

Virtually no included studies systematically reported standardized geriatric assessment tools or frailty indices (such as the G8 screening tool or modified Frailty Index), masking the critical distinction between chronological and biological age.
The International Society of Geriatric Oncology (SIOG) and the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) mandate formal geriatric assessments for all oncology patients aged 65 and older (49).

text.text: Both the NCCN and ASCO require the integration of these assessments directly into chemotherapy counseling and therapeutic decisionmaking (4).
SIOG advocates for comprehensive geriatric evaluation to identify and manage occult physiological deficits in older cancer patients.

To operationalize this, the American College of Surgeons and the American Geriatric Society established bestpractice guidelines designed to flag high-risk surgical candidates, mitigate perioperative complications, and optimize surgical care (18).
text.formatted: To operationalize this, the American College of Surgeons and the American Geriatric Society established bestpractice guidelines designed to flag high-risk surgical candidates, mitigate perioperative complications, and optimize surgical care <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Standard guidelines continue to recommend primary debulking surgery followed by platinum-based chemotherapy for fit patients.
However, tumor boards must strongly consider NACT for poor surgical candidates or those with a low probability of achieving optimal cytoreduction.
The definition of a poor surgical candidate explicitly includes patients with advanced age, documented frailty, degraded performance status, or severe medical comorbidities (16).
text.formatted: The definition of a poor surgical candidate explicitly includes patients with advanced age, documented frailty, degraded performance status, or severe medical comorbidities <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Joint clinical practice guidelines from the Society of Gynecologic Oncology (SGO) and ASCO, established in 2016, clearly delineate these management pathways for advanced disease (14, 45).
text.formatted: Joint clinical practice guidelines from the Society of Gynecologic Oncology (SGO) and ASCO, established in 2016, clearly delineate these management pathways for advanced disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">45)</ref>.

text.text: In contemporary medical oncology, clinicians utilize a stepwise evaluation process, initiating assessment with rapid frailty screening instruments like the G8.

Multidisciplinary geriatric co-management delivers measurable value to all older surgical patients, extending beyond the frail population, and institutions should deploy these services as broadly as possible across the geriatric surgical cohort (7).
text.formatted: Multidisciplinary geriatric co-management delivers measurable value to all older surgical patients, extending beyond the frail population, and institutions should deploy these services as broadly as possible across the geriatric surgical cohort <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Future clinical trials evaluating surgical timing in advanced ovarian cancer must mandate the inclusion of older adults.
Trial designs should transition away from arbitrary chronological age thresholds and instead stratify treatment arms based on validated, multidimensional frailty indices.
Prospective validation is required to determine whether targeted prehabilitation prior to NACT-IDS can further optimize R0 resection rates and mitigate sarcopenia in the geriatric population.
For older adults with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, NACT-IDS represents the safest and most effective initial management strategy.
Upfront primary debulking surgery in patients over the age of 70 carries substantial risks of catastrophic surgical morbidity and early mortality.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy successfully downstages disease, maximizes the probability of achieving complete macroscopic clearance, and significantly protects physiological reserve.
Until prospective randomized trials stratifying patients by biological frailty are completed, NACT-IDS should be strongly considered as the standard of care for the geriatric demographic.

Downgraded 1 level for Serious Confounding by Indication: Observational registry cohorts inherently suffer from channeling bias where frailer patients are directed to chemotherapy rather than upfront radical surgery.
